title: Alien Dictionary
description: Brute force to optimized: comparing every pair of words versus extracting constraints from adjacent pairs and topologically sorting.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a list of words sorted lexicographically according to the rules of an unknown alien alphabet, derive a valid ordering of the letters in that alien alphabet, or return an empty string if no valid ordering is possible (invalid input or a contradiction).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Comparing two ADJACENT words in the sorted list, their FIRST differing character directly reveals that the letter from the earlier word must come before the letter from the later word in the alien alphabet (a directed edge). Comparing NON-adjacent words provides no NEW information beyond what is already implied by the chain of adjacent comparisons. Collecting all such edges from every adjacent pair and running a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) produces a valid letter ordering, or reveals impossibility if a cycle exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reconstructing an Unknown Alphabet's Order From a Sorted Phone Book
blocks.text: Picture a phone book sorted according to some UNKNOWN alphabet ordering. Comparing each pair of adjacent names, their first point of difference reveals exactly one letter-ordering fact (which letter comes first). Collecting all these facts and arranging them consistently reconstructs the entire unknown alphabet's order, or reveals a contradiction if the facts conflict.

blocks.caption: Each adjacent word pair's first differing character reveals a direct ordering edge between two letters

blocks.text: Result: "" (z comes before x from the first pair, but x before z is implied later, a contradiction, empty result).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every letter appearing anywhere in the input becomes a node in a directed graph, regardless of whether any ordering constraint involves it yet.

Observation 2: For each ADJACENT pair of words, find their FIRST differing character position; the letter from the earlier word must precede the letter from the later word, an edge in the graph. If NO differing character is found and the earlier word is LONGER than the later word, this is an invalid input (a longer word cannot correctly sort before its own prefix), return empty immediately.

Observation 3: Running Kahn's algorithm (BFS via in-degrees) on this graph produces a valid ordering of ALL letters, or reveals that some letters never get processed (a cycle, meaning contradictory constraints), which correctly signals impossibility.

Observation 4: The final ordering must include every letter that appeared anywhere in the input, not just those directly involved in an ordering constraint.
This leads to extracting ordering edges from adjacent word pairs, then running Kahn's algorithm (topological sort) over all letters.
Compare EVERY pair of words (not just adjacent ones) to extract ordering constraints, redundantly re-deriving information already implied by adjacent comparisons.
Why the code is written this way

items: Comparing every pair of words directly extracts ordering constraints thoroughly.
This is redundant: since words are sorted, ADJACENT comparisons already imply every ordering fact that non-adjacent comparisons would reveal, making the extra comparisons unnecessary work.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(words squared times word length).
Space: O(distinct letter pairs) for the edge set.
Limitation: comparing only ADJACENT word pairs (not every pair) extracts the exact same complete set of ordering constraints, at a fraction of the cost.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Collect every distinct letter appearing in any word as a graph node. For each ADJACENT pair of words, find their first differing character; add a directed edge from the earlier word's letter to the later word's letter (if not already present, to avoid double-counting in-degree), and increment the target letter's in-degree. If no differing character exists and the earlier word is longer, return an empty string immediately (invalid). After processing all adjacent pairs, run Kahn's algorithm: seed a queue with every zero-in-degree letter, process it, appending it to the result and decrementing its neighbors' in-degrees, enqueueing any that reach zero. If the final result includes every letter, return it; otherwise, return an empty string (a cycle exists).
Extract ordering edges from adjacent word pairs only, then run Kahn's algorithm over all letters.

blocks.text: Since the input words are ALREADY sorted by the alien alphabet, comparing only ADJACENT pairs extracts every distinct ordering fact implied by the entire sorted list (a non-adjacent pair's ordering is always transitively implied by the chain of adjacent comparisons between them); running Kahn's algorithm on the resulting graph correctly produces a valid topological order respecting every extracted constraint, or reveals a cycle (contradictory constraints) if not every letter can be processed, correctly signaling an impossible/invalid input.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(total characters across all words).
Space: O(distinct letters plus edges) for the graph.

blocks.text: Alien Dictionary combines two ideas cleanly: extracting ordering constraints from ADJACENT sorted-list comparisons only, then a standard topological sort to resolve them.

items: Comparing every pair of words instead of just adjacent ones, wasting effort on already-implied information.
Forgetting the special invalid case: if a word is a PREFIX of, but comes AFTER, a longer version of itself, no valid ordering can exist.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "derive an ordering rule from a list already sorted by that unknown rule", think: extract pairwise constraints from adjacent comparisons, then topologically sort.

items: How would you detect and report specifically WHICH letters are involved in a contradiction, not just that one exists?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The all-pairs comparison approach costs O(words squared times length); the adjacent-pairs-only approach costs O(total characters), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: extract pairwise ordering constraints from adjacent sorted-list comparisons, then topologically sort.
Core Idea: the first differing character between adjacent words reveals exactly one directed ordering edge; only adjacent pairs are needed.
Time: O(words squared times length) for the brute force, O(total characters) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(letter pairs) for the brute force, O(letters plus edges) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: adjacent comparisons alone capture every ordering constraint implied by the full sorted list.
Interview Difficulty: a hard, classic combination of comparison-extraction and topological sort.
One line memory trick: adjacent pairs give edges; topological sort gives the order.
